dedupe_keys.name: solar storm risk to the north american electric grid lloyd s and aer 2013 county level relative risk and carrington level outage scenarios

description: This 2013 report by the insurance market Lloyd's, with research by the firm Atmospheric and Environmental Research, assesses how an extreme geomagnetic storm could damage the North American power grid. The 21-page report read on 2026-09-28 estimates storm return periods from auroral records, about 50 years for a Quebec 1989 level storm and 150 years for a Carrington-level event, then combines magnetic latitude, ground conductivity, distance to the coast and transmission line length into a relative risk score by county, and runs a dynamic assessment with a Carrington-level storm time series, a power grid model, transformer ages and internal heating to derive damage criteria and outage scenarios. Its results put 20 to 40 million people in the United States at risk of outages lasting 16 days to one or two years, at a cost of 0.6 to 2.6 trillion US dollars, with the highest population-weighted risk between Washington and New York. Coverage is the United States and Canada. Access is free as a PDF, under all rights reserved copyright. Caveats: the grid model and county scores are described but not published as data, and the numbers reflect 2013 grid conditions. It shows how to chain hazard, conductivity and transformer vulnerability into a cascading failure and loss estimate for an insurance-scale scenario. Related records: the later Lloyd's and Cambridge space weather scenario, the Hydro-Québec 1989 blackout and the USArray magnetotelluric data.

name: Solar Storm Risk to the North American Electric Grid (Lloyd's and AER, 2013): county-level relative risk and Carrington-level outage scenarios
outcomes: A Carrington-level storm could leave 20 to 40 million people in the US without power for 16 days to 1 to 2 years, at an estimated 0.6 to 2.6 trillion USD; highest population-weighted risk along the Atlantic corridor from Washington DC to New York City, then the Midwest and Gulf Coast; weaker storms could damage around 10 to 20 transformers; replacement lead time at least five months.
provider: Lloyd's of London with Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Inc. (AER)
resources_used: magnetic latitude, ground conductivity and coast effect factors
power grid model with transformer age distribution and internal heating
